claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by optimization of the nanoparticles' atomic-scale configuration.
Combining in situ characterization with atomistic simulations can optimize the atomic-scale configuration.
The initial near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles have an FCC crystal structure.
The nanoparticles will be heated to 973 K at 5 K/min and annealed isothermally for 2 hours.
MD and DFT simulations will model atomic-scale configurations and predict nanoparticle stability.
High vacuum or an Ar environment minimizes oxidation and contamination.
The relevant structural mediator is the arrangement of atoms, vacancies, and dislocations.
Heating induces atomic diffusion and rearrangement.
Thermally induced diffusion and rearrangement optimize the atomic-scale configuration.
Optimization of the atomic-scale configuration enhances structural and chemical stability.
The intervention will increase nanoparticle stability by 20% relative to the baseline.
The intervention will improve catalytic reaction rates by 15% relative to the baseline.
Reduced oxidation and contamination provide a measure of nanoparticle stability.
The proposed mechanism applies across 773–1173 K for catalytic operation.
The proposed mechanism applies across 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use.
The proposed boundary includes nanoparticles containing less than 10 at.% noble metal.
Failure to increase both stability and catalytic activity by at least 10% relative to baseline falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure of the atomic-scale configuration to optimize during heating and annealing falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: A 10^-9 mbar high-vacuum environment and an Ar atmosphere are presented as simultaneous conditions, although a substantive Ar atmosphere is incompatible with maintaining that vacuum unless they are intended as separate experimental arms.
